extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and criteria for determining patent infringement, focusing on substantial identity, mechanical equivalents, product vs process issues, and how courts and juries should assess similarity and substitution. Includes examples and case law illustrating when a substituted part or altered form nonetheless infringes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical equivalents doctrine (identity of purpose over form)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine depends upon the truth that the identity of purpose, and not of form or name, is the true criterion in judging of the similarity or dissimilarity of two pieces of mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The question whether one thing is a mechanical equivalent for another is a question of fact for the jury, on the testimony of experts, or an inspection of the machines; it is an inference to be drawn from all the circumstances of the case. Consider whether the contrivance used by the defendant is used for the same purpose, performs the same duties, or is applicable to the same object as the contrivance used by the patentee. If so, there is infringement even if embodied in a form not described or claimed by the patentee. (Includes cases: Winans v. Denmead, Morgan v. Seaward.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial identity / substantial embodiment of patentee's mode
rubrics_metrics.description: To infringe, the defendant's article must be so near the patentee's form as to substantially embody the patentee's mode of operation and thereby attain the same kind of result as was reached by his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that the defendant employ the invention to as good advantage or attain precisely the same degree of result; the result must be the same in kind and effected by substantially the same mode of operation. (Example: circular vs octagonal car — octagonal held substantially the same as circular where it achieved same practical uses.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Form vs substance separability (look-through-form principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where form and substance are inseparable, it is enough to look at the form only. Where they are separable, where the whole substance of the invention may be copied in a different form, courts and juries must look through the form for the substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the form only embodies the invention (inseparable), only that form is covered; if the substance can be embodied in varied forms, those varied forms may infringe. (Explanation and examples throughout the text including Davis v. Palmer and the Stevens/Donkin discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of claiming a particular form or element
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee describes and claims a particular form or element, and that form alone is capable of embodying the invention, the patent covers only that geometrical form; if the form is not copied, the invention is not used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a specification insists on a particular component (e.g., a 'crank'), the court must determine whether the defendant's substitute (e.g., an eccentric axis with a collar) is the same thing in principle or merely a variation; relative terms may have reference to particular pieces of machinery and the specification's particularity affects the infringement inquiry (see Morgan v. Seaward discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Known mechanical substitute (Sawyer's definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: "When in mechanics one device does a particular thing... every other device known and used in mechanics, which skilful and experienced workmen know will produce the same result, or do the same particular thing, is a known mechanical substitute..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is sufficient that a skilled mechanic, on seeing one device do a particular thing, knows that other devices, whose uses he is acquainted with, will do the same thing. This defines the class of substitutes that courts treat as equivalents for infringement purposes (Carter v. Baker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical equivalent that also yields an improvement still infringes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant's change is a mechanical equivalent of the patentee's means and also accomplishes some other advantage beyond the patentee's effect or purpose, it is still an infringement as respects what is covered by the patent, though the further advantage may be patentable as an improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using the earth as a return circuit in telegraphy was a mere equivalent for the return wire in connection with the patented signalling machinery and thus an infringement of the patentee's rights, even if the earth-return circuit might itself support a separate patent as an improvement (Electric Telegraph Co. v. Brett).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements by defendant do not excuse infringement when principle identical
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant's machine is the same in principle as the patentee's machine, it is no defence that the defendant has improved it, no matter to what extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law discriminates and may grant exclusive property to both the original inventor and the improver, but neither may use the other's discovery without a license. Thus improvements remain infringements as to the original principle (Perkins/Read example; Alden v. Dewy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Names and forms are of comparatively little importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Names as well as the forms of things are of comparatively little importance; the critical question is whether, under variation of form or a thing with a different name, the defendant accomplishes the same purpose, object, or effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on what the defendant's device accomplishes in substance rather than on labels or superficial differences in form (illustrated across cited authorities and jury instructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question of infringement and mechanical equivalence is a question of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether something is a mechanical equivalent and whether there has been infringement is a question of fact for the jury to determine from the evidence, expert testimony, and inspection of the machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges instruct juries to compare the principles of operation, consider expert views, and assess whether differences are merely colorable or truly material (see Morgan v. Seaward jury instruction quoted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture patents — substantial identity test applies
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject-matter of the patent is a manufacture, the same test of substantial identity is applied: whether in reality and in substance the defendant has availed himself of the invention of the patentee to make the fabric or article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Varying the process of application or incidental circumstances will not avoid infringement if the defendant has taken the same plan and applied it to the same purpose. Example: Walton v. Potter (carding teeth with india-rubber) and Goodyear disputes about the essential agent in vulcanization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of appearance/structure as presumptive evidence of same process
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity in appearance and structure will not of itself always establish infringement where the patent is for a process; but similarity of structure of two things is presumptive evidence of their being made in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the patent covers a manufactured article but the claim is a process, courts infer that similar-appearing products were made by the same process only by drawing inferences from the evidence; similarity is presumptive, not conclusive (Lord Ellenborough rule cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying with intent to evade (slight variation disregarded)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the imitation is so nearly exact as to satisfy the jury that the imitator attempted to copy the model and made some almost imperceptible variation for the purpose of evading the patentee's right, such slight variation may be disregarded as fraud upon the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where evidence indicates an attempt to evade the patentee by cosmetic or insubstantial changes, courts will treat the device as an infringement despite the minor variations (cited cases: Davis v. Palmer and others).
